newsitem.title: USA: Early US Midwest corn high in moisture and damage.
newsitem.headline: Early US Midwest corn high in moisture and damage.

text.p: Early harvested corn in Illinois and Indiana contained high moisture, kernel damage, and debris, resulting in farmers being penalized when the grain was sold, grain dealers and agronomists said.

The price incentive for selling corn early is substantial. In southern Indiana, where corn harvest just began, corn delivered this week will return about $3.65 per bushel, for next week delivery about $3.55, and the week after that $3.45. Corn for October delivery was bid $3.26.

"There is about a 40-cent premium for corn (delivered now versus October)," said Dan Wiener, a grain merchandiser with Gibson Consolidated Terminals in Princeton, Ind. "It is a big incentive for these guys."

However, grain dealers in Illinois and Indiana said the high moisture, filth, and damaged kernels are drawing stiff price penalties and erasing much if not all the price advantages the farmers were aiming for. Wiener said in one instance, a farmer faced penalities of about 65 cents a bushel.
"People are harvesting wet corn at 30 to 35 percent moisture," said Walker Kirby, an extension specialist in the University of Illinois Department of Crop Sciences.
Kirby reported a similar incident in Illinois where a farmer was penalized for damaged grain.
"He was mad because he was being docked for all this stuff," Kirby said of the debris and high moisture.
In addition to high moisture, Kirby said high incidences of ear rot in southern Illinois have resulted in cob fragments mixing with the grain.
"Elevator people are telling me a lot of corn coming in is chewed up," said Terry Keeneth, a Gibson County, Ind., agriculture educator with the Purdue University Cooperative Extension Service.
The grain is being damaged when farmers use mechanical dryers to reduce the moisture content to near the preferred 15 percent.
But Keeneth said farmers were pleased with early yields in that southwest Indiana county.
"Farmers are telling me they are getting decent yields of 150 to 160 bushels from the early fields," he said.
But moisture levels of 22 to 24 percent were common, requiring mechanical drying to about 15 percent.
Agricultural statistics services in Illinois and Indiana reported Monday that the corn harvest was in its early stages in southern portions of those states.
Kirby said corn in central and northern Illinois was in better shape than in the south, but was developing late and may be damaged by frost before it can be harvested.
The harvest in southeast Missouri was progressing and some counties reported 60 percent was done. High yields and good quality have been common.
"The quality is good. We are getting some 60-lb test weights," said a Mississippi County, Mo., grain dealer.
